Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Agricultural Worker
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Nadia is a 34-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment after more than a year of trying to manage on her own. She is divorced and works long days as an agricultural worker, moving between fields, packing sheds, and shared work areas where conversations travel easily and people are constantly coming and going. The event she returns to began during a workday when she witnessed a violent trauma involving another person. What remains most vivid to her is not a single orderly memory but the atmosphere of danger around it: the sudden shift in people’s faces, the sense that something was wrong before anyone said it out loud, the sound of a baby crying nearby while adults began shouting over each other. She remembers watching someone who had seemed ordinary moments earlier become frightening, and afterward she could not shake the feeling that threat announces itself in small, unreadable changes that other people miss until it is too late.

In the weeks after, Nadia told herself she had to stay strong and get on with work. She made a deliberate effort to think in bright, disciplined phrases—everything is fine, it could have been worse, just focus on the good—because she felt that allowing herself to dwell on what she had seen would be dangerous. When images or fragments of the scene came into her mind, she pushed them away quickly and sharply, as if refusing them entry. She described doing this almost automatically, especially at night or on the drive to work. At the same time, she began cleaning with an intensity that surprised even her. She would come home and reorganize kitchen shelves, wipe counters repeatedly, sort and re-sort drawers, and continue long after the apartment was already clean. The repetition gave her a brief sense that things could still be put in order.

Her world gradually became organized around moments that felt charged. At work, if two coworkers lowered their voices or exchanged a look she could not read, Nadia’s body would tense before she had fully registered why. She found herself watching for people who seemed “off,” studying their movements, tone, and expressions. She had come to believe that people are not what they seem and that the most dangerous person in a setting may be the one everyone else is overlooking. Ordinary conversations in the fields or break area could suddenly become unbearable if they turned toward violence, crime, family tragedy, or anything that echoed the circumstances of what she witnessed. When that happened, she would walk away to check equipment, volunteer for a different task, or busy herself with sorting produce rather than remain where she had to hear it.

Babies’ cries were especially potent. In public, in workers’ housing nearby, even hearing a baby from a passing car could stop her mid-thought and bring back the helpless, exposed feeling of that day. She did not describe this in abstract terms; she said it felt as if the air changed around her, as if she were again bracing for something terrible to unfold in front of her. Because agricultural work often places her near other families and laborers, these moments were difficult to avoid entirely. On days when she heard a baby crying near the packing area or in the distance from neighboring housing, she became preoccupied and distracted, then ashamed that she could not simply ignore it.

Over time Nadia’s view of herself in the world narrowed and hardened. She spoke with sadness about having lost faith—not only in other people but in life itself, and in the sense that there is any larger goodness watching over events. Since her divorce she had already felt unmoored, but after the trauma that feeling deepened into a conviction that she no longer belonged anywhere. She no longer felt fully at ease with coworkers, did not want to confide in family, and found little comfort in the beliefs or community practices that had once steadied her. Being around others often left her feeling separate, as if everyone else were participating in a world whose basic safety she no longer accepted.

What finally brought Nadia to seek help was not one dramatic crisis but exhaustion. She was tired of spending so much energy forcing herself to think positively, tired of batting memories away, tired of cleaning late into the night for a few minutes of relief. More than once at work she had caught herself leaving a conversation abruptly because the topic turned in a direction she could not bear, and she worried others were noticing her withdrawal. She came in saying she did not want to live like someone always scanning, always organizing, always pretending. What frightened her most was the possibility that she would never again trust anyone or feel that she belonged anywhere. What she hoped for, though she said it cautiously, was to feel less on guard in her own life.
